power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence

author.affiliation:
New York University
								
									New York
									USA

Sapienza University of Rome
								
									Rome
									Italy

text.text: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs.
Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence.
Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation.
More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all.
Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities.
AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us.

We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI's effects on human welfare.
In 1950, Alan Turing proposed replacing the question "Can machines think?"
with a question about whether a computer could succeed in an imitation game (1).
text.formatted: with a question about whether a computer could succeed in an imitation game <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: In the standard three-party version, an informed interrogator communicates by text with two hidden respondents, one human and one machine, and then guesses which respondent is human (2, 3).
text.formatted: In the standard three-party version, an informed interrogator communicates by text with two hidden respondents, one human and one machine, and then guesses which respondent is human <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3)</ref>.

text.text: Recent advances in large language models have revived interest in the test .
Claims that AI has passed, or even "broken", the test have also appeared in Nature (39), the New York Post (40), and Psychology Today (41).
text.formatted: Claims that AI has passed, or even "broken", the test have also appeared in Nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(39)</ref>, the New York Post <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref>, and Psychology Today <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(41)</ref>.

text.text: Here we argue that human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence.
A system may reproduce human answers in a particular test without possessing the capacities those answers appear to demonstrate.
We further argue that convincing imitation is itself the wrong goal for AI.
We identified 35 papers applying the Turing-test label on LLMs, of which 16 were classified as reporting positive results under their respective criteria (Table 1).
text.formatted: We identified 35 papers applying the Turing-test label on LLMs, of which 16 were classified as reporting positive results under their respective criteria (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The largest category evaluates pre-generated texts or scripted responses through judgments of authorship, humanlikeness, or quality .

Other designs examine covert insertion of AI-written examination answers into university assessments (34), automated detection of generated language (35, 36), vision-and-language tasks (37), recorded speech dialogues (38), chatbot choices in economic games (10, 11), two-party conversations (6-8), and self-directed dialogue (9).
text.formatted: Other designs examine covert insertion of AI-written examination answers into university assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34)</ref>, automated detection of generated language <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36)</ref>, vision-and-language tasks (37), recorded speech dialogues <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(38)</ref>, chatbot choices in economic games <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>, two-party conversations (6-8), and self-directed dialogue <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>.

text.text: Only three papers include standard three-party conversations (4-6), and only one reports a pass in that format.
Jones and Bergen found that GPT-4.5, prompted to adopt a humanlike persona, was selected as human in 73% of five-minute trials (4).
We recognize this as a substantial achievement in conversational impersonation.
The central question nevertheless remains: which cognitive capacities does this success establish, and how far do they extend?
Despite their procedural diversity, these studies share a common focus on the mimicry of human outputs, rather than examining underlying cognitive processes.
Success is assessed against what humans produce or what judges perceive as human.
Crucially, similarity in outputs does not imply similarity in the processes that produce them (42) (43) (44) (45).
text.formatted: Crucially, similarity in outputs does not imply similarity in the processes that produce them <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(43)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(44)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(45)</ref>.

text.text: Loru and colleagues, for example, found differences in the observable criteria guiding human and LLM evaluations of news-source credibility, despite some agreement in their judgments (42).
text.formatted: Loru and colleagues, for example, found differences in the observable criteria guiding human and LLM evaluations of news-source credibility, despite some agreement in their judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, a humanlike answer on a particular test leaves open how the system arrived at that answer and whether the competence it appears to demonstrate extends to other problems.
A fundamental distinction is between linguistic proficiency and broader cognition.

Evidence from neuroscience is particularly illuminating: some individuals with severe aphasia retain abilities such as arithmetic and causal reasoning despite profound impairments in language comprehension and production (46, 47).
text.formatted: Evidence from neuroscience is particularly illuminating: some individuals with severe aphasia retain abilities such as arithmetic and causal reasoning despite profound impairments in language comprehension and production <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(46,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47)</ref>.

text.text: During autoregressive pretraining, LLMs are optimized to assign higher probabilities to the next tokens observed in their training data.
This objective rewards accurate prediction of linguistic sequences.
It does not directly reward reasoning.
Which reasoning capacities emerge, and how general they are, must therefore be established empirically.
Generalization concerns whether competence extends to unfamiliar instances and contexts.
Success on difficult questions does not guarantee this.
In fact, errors on comparatively easy questions and sensitivity to alternative phrasings persist in increasingly capable LLMs (48).
text.formatted: In fact, errors on comparatively easy questions and sensitivity to alternative phrasings persist in increasingly capable LLMs <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(48)</ref>.

text.text: Humans also make mistakes, but their patterns of error may differ systematically from those of machines (49).
text.formatted: Humans also make mistakes, but their patterns of error may differ systematically from those of machines <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(49)</ref>.

text.text: Differences may also concern when humans and machines suspend judgment (respond "I don't know").
Evaluations should establish whether a system generalizes reliably, recognizes the limits of its competence, and withholds judgment when the evidence is insufficient.
Dynamic problems pose a further challenge.
Many real-world problems unfold over time, requiring agents to reconsider what the problem actually is.
An important but often neglected dimension of intelligence is adaptive reframing: revising how a problem is represented in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context (50).
text.formatted: An important but often neglected dimension of intelligence is adaptive reframing: revising how a problem is represented in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(50)</ref>.

text.text: Evaluations should establish whether an agent recognizes the need for such a revision without being explicitly instructed to reframe.
Thus, existing Turing tests focus on human likeness in specific tasks.

But yet, even if future tests probe human-like reasoning, generalization, and adaptability, we believe the problem runs deeper: why should "human mimicry at the output level" be the benchmark for artificial intelligence in the first place?
Understanding whether LLMs and other AI systems can imitate human behavior is scientifically valuable.
It can reveal the conditions under which people recognize artificial agents and the vulnerabilities that arise when they cannot.
However, human-like behavior should not be the central goal for artificial intelligence.

Our judgments are vulnerable to systematic biases (51), our limited attention and memory often compromise how we interpret evidence and make decisions (52), and negative emotions can sometimes have harmful consequences (53).
text.formatted: Our judgments are vulnerable to systematic biases (51), our limited attention and memory often compromise how we interpret evidence and make decisions (52), and negative emotions can sometimes have harmful consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(53)</ref>.

text.text: AI systems that reproduce our decisions may amplify harmful consequences through repeated interaction (54).
text.formatted: AI systems that reproduce our decisions may amplify harmful consequences through repeated interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(54)</ref>.

text.text: Convincing human imitation could also introduce opportunities for manipulation.
A system that reliably impersonates a person could appear to be an independent adviser, sympathetic confidant, or fellow citizen while covertly serving commercial or political interests (55).
text.formatted: A system that reliably impersonates a person could appear to be an independent adviser, sympathetic confidant, or fellow citizen while covertly serving commercial or political interests <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(55)</ref>.

text.text: Fluent assistance can also undermine the judgment it is meant to support.
In experiments deliberately using incorrect AI advice, access to that advice reduced participants' willingness to say "I don't know", lowered accuracy, and increased confidence (56).
text.formatted: In experiments deliberately using incorrect AI advice, access to that advice reduced participants' willingness to say "I don't know", lowered accuracy, and increased confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(56)</ref>.

text.text: In other experiments, misaligned AI led people to factually incorrect or suboptimal answers (57, 58).
text.formatted: In other experiments, misaligned AI led people to factually incorrect or suboptimal answers <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(57,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58)</ref>.

text.text: There might also be economic risks.

Brynjolfsson's "Turing trap" warns that an excessive focus on replicating human work can favor replacement over augmentation, weakening workers' bargaining power and concentrating wealth and influence among those who control the technology (59).
text.formatted: Brynjolfsson's "Turing trap" warns that an excessive focus on replicating human work can favor replacement over augmentation, weakening workers' bargaining power and concentrating wealth and influence among those who control the technology <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(59)</ref>.

text.text: Reason, science, and institutions have helped people cooperate and curb destructive impulses (60, 61).
text.formatted: Reason, science, and institutions have helped people cooperate and curb destructive impulses <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(60,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61)</ref>.

text.text: AI should support these achievements by helping us correct errors, expand scientific understanding, and make informed choices.
We should aim to build systems that enlarge what people can accomplish while preserving their ability to question, deliberate, and choose.
We should judge their success by whether they help more people know more, suffer less, and exercise greater control over their lives.
We recommend coordinated changes in AI design, funding, and deployment, with institutional incentives rewarding systems that expand human capabilities while preserving independent judgment.
At the development level, companies should prioritize augmenting human capabilities over replacing people.
The goal should be to improve human judgment and performance, rather than merely reproduce human outputs and encourage uncritical reliance.
For example, systems should communicate uncertainty in ways validated against actual performance and promote independent verification and critical thinking.
Funders should translate these design priorities into explicit criteria for support.

For example, they should require funded projects to assess how benefits and costs are distributed, including effects on access to expertise, workers' autonomy, and the concentration of economic gains.
They should also prioritize proposals that enable users to scrutinize evidence and challenge recommendations, with explicit plans to test whether these features improve human judgment.
Institutions should reinforce these incentives through procurement and renewal decisions guided by evidence of benefit.

For example, AI evaluations should test relevant capacities beyond imitation, including generalization, appropriate suspension of judgment, and the ability to reframe problems as circumstances change.
Evaluations should also compare assisted with unaided performance, measuring accuracy, confidence calibration, and users' ability to detect and reject incorrect advice.
Human likeness may remain a legitimate object of scientific study, but investment and deployment decisions should be guided by demonstrated benefits to people.
